```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
```

Producing a sibling-survival mortality estimate from a DHS or MICS file requires
a long series of small decisions: which reported siblings enter the analysis,
where the observation window starts and stops, whether the month a sibling died
counts as exposure, which questionnaire codes make a death pregnancy-related,
and what age distribution the rates are standardised by. Most of these are
undocumented in the survey reports, and several of them move published numbers
by more than the substantive differences anyone is trying to measure.

This document sets out every one of those decisions, what each instrument
actually gives you, and what The DHS Program and UNICEF do with it in the code
that produces their own report tables. **It is written to be usable without this
package** --- in Stata, SPSS, Python or anything else --- so each decision is
stated in terms of the questionnaire variables. Where `siblingsurvival`
implements the decision, a closing line names the function and argument that
controls it.

There is a section for the DHS and a section for MICS, because the two
instruments differ enough that a single merged treatment obscures more than it
saves. A short closing section covers the places where the two disagree with
each other, which matters if you are putting DHS and MICS surveys into one
analysis.


## The two reference implementations

Neither the DHS reports nor the MICS reports document these conventions. Both
organisations, however, publish the code that produced the tables, and that code
is the authority used throughout this document.

**DHS.** [`DHS-Indicators-Stata`](https://github.com/DHSProgram/DHS-Indicators-Stata),
directory `Chap16_AM`. The substantive file is `AM_rates.do` (1,376 lines,
Thomas Pullum, with modifications by Trevor Croft and Shireen Assaf). Its header
states that it *"agrees exactly with DHS procedures, except for confidence
intervals"* and that it is *"a complete re-write, not a translation, of the
CSPro program"*. Unusually for code of this kind, it explains its reasoning in
prose as it goes. The companion *Guide to DHS Statistics*, chapter "Adult and
Maternal Mortality", is cited by `AM_rates.do` directly on at least one
substantive point, so the two should be read together. Both are public and need
no registration. Line numbers cited below are from this file.

**MICS.** `MICS6 - 06 - TM.9.1&TM.9.2&TM.9.3&DQ.7.1&DQ7.2.sps` (v02, 2020-04-14),
from the MICS6 "42 Syntax Files" distribution. It produces the whole mortality
table group in one pass. It is much terser than the DHS file and explains
nothing, but it is unambiguous about what it computes.

Literal transcriptions of both into R live in this repository, at
`data-raw/dhs-validation/stata-reference-replica.R` and
`data-raw/mics-validation/spss-syntax-replica.R`. They are not part of the
package. They exist so that a gap between any implementation and a published
table can be attributed to a named convention rather than guessed at, and that
is what most of the evidence quoted below comes from.


## Decision index

Every decision in this document, with the two answers side by side. Rows marked
⚠ are ones where the DHS and MICS answers genuinely differ, so a combined
analysis has to choose.

| | Decision | DHS | MICS |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Unusable sex code | drop (`mm1` > 2) | drop (`MM15` 8/9) |
| 2 | Unknown survival status | drop (`mm2` > 1) | ⚠ reference **keeps**, with full exposure |
| 3 | Don't-know on numeric items | system-missing | ⚠ coded **98/99**, not missing |
| 4 | Observation window | `[doi - 84, doi - 1]` | `[wdoi - 84, wdoi - 1]` |
| 5 | Month of interview | excluded | excluded |
| 6 | Boundary convention | left-closed, right-open | left-closed, right-open |
| 7 | Month of death as exposure | ⚠ **counted** (`last = mm8`) | ⚠ **not counted** (`MM18C - 1`) |
| 8 | Age group of a death | age at that month, from date of birth | age at that month, from date of birth |
| 9 | Birth and death dates | `mm4` / `mm8`, always coded | `MM17C` / `MM18C` when present, else derive |
| 10 | Pregnancy-related | `mm9` in 2--6 --- **two months** | `MM22`/`MM23`/`MM24` --- two months |
| 11 | Published pregnancy-related | ⚠ two-month count | ⚠ **42-day** count (`MM25 < 42`) |
| 12 | Maternal | `mm9` 2--5, `mm16` not 1 or 2 | 42-day, not `MM26`/`MM27`; MICS6/7 only |
| 13 | Time-since-delivery band | `mm12` **not used** | no analogue |
| 14 | 2016 PRMR recode | documented, not executed | no analogue |
| 15 | Weights | `v005` / 1,000,000 | `wmweight`, already mean 1 |
| 16 | All-woman factor | `awfactt` / 100, on the age distribution | no analogue |
| 17 | Standardisation population | respondents, **both sexes** | respondents (completed interviews) |
| 18 | Life table `nax` | 2.6 | 2.6 |

# Part 1: DHS

The DHS sibling history is an optional module in the women's questionnaire. It
is published in the individual recode (`IR`) file, **wide**: one row per
respondent, and one column per roster item per sibling, so `mm1_01`, `mm1_02`,
… up to the maximum sibship size in the survey. The practical test of whether a
survey has the module is whether the `IR` file has `mm`-prefixed columns.

Two variants matter. DHS phases 2 through 5 carry roster items `mm1`--`mm15`;
phases 6 through 8 add `mm16`, the violence/accident item --- though in practice
`mm16` was only introduced from 2016 onwards, so a phase-7 survey fielded before
then does not have it. Of the 43 surveys with a roster examined here, only five
carry `mm16` at all.


## 1.1 Which reported siblings enter the analysis

### Sex

`mm1` is coded 1 male, 2 female. It is **not** a clean binary: the DHS labels 8
as "don't know", and some surveys carry an unlabelled 9 --- Gabon 2000 has 163
of them.

The reference drops them outright (`:305`, `drop if mm1 > 2`).

The obvious shortcut, `sex = ifelse(mm1 == 2, "female", "male")`, is the
dangerous version, because every unusable code silently becomes male. Doing that
inflated male exposure in **13 of the 43** surveys, by up to 0.7%, and put
siblings of unknown sex into the male rates. It went unnoticed for a long time
precisely because female results were unaffected --- every female quantity
matched the reference exactly while the male ones did not.

*In this package:* `get_sib_df()` maps 1 to `'m'`, 2 to `'f'` and everything
else to `NA`; `finalize_sib_prep()` drops those rows and counts them in
`summ$miss.sex`.

### Survival status

`mm2` is 1 alive, 0 dead, 8 don't know. The reference drops the don't-knows
(`:328`, `drop if mm2 > 1`).

This is one of the few places where the DHS and MICS references agree in
substance but not in practice --- see §2.1, where MICS keeps them.

*In this package:* dropped unless `keep_missing = TRUE`.

### Siblings who cannot be placed

A sibling with no usable date of birth cannot be assigned to an age group at
all, so contributes neither exposure nor events. The same is true of a sibling
whose respondent has no sampling weight --- rare, but real: one respondent in
São Tomé and Príncipe 2014 has none.

These are worth dropping explicitly rather than leaving in, because a single one
turns an entire exposure cell into `NA` when the cell is summed, which is silent
and looks like a far larger problem than it is.

*In this package:* dropped by `finalize_sib_prep()`, reported as `summ$miss.dob`
and `summ$miss.wgt`.

### A caveat about entirely empty columns

A roster column can be present and completely missing. **Burkina Faso 2003 has
an `mm9` column in which all 249,540 values are missing**, so no
pregnancy-related death can be identified and the count is exactly zero. Both
this package and the DHS reference produce that zero silently. A zero
pregnancy-related mortality rate reads as a finding rather than as a survey that
never coded the module, so it is worth testing for.

It is the only such survey of the 43, and whether it belongs in an analysis
sample is a decision for the analyst.

*In this package:* `add_maternal_deaths()` warns.


## 1.2 The observation window

With the documented defaults `lw = -6, uw = 0`, `AM_rates.do:230-231` computes

```
start_month = doi + 12*lw - 12   ->  doi - 84
end_month   = doi + 12*uw - 1    ->  doi - 1
```

so the window is the 84 months ending the month **before** the interview. The
file says why: *"As is standard DHS practice, exposure or events in the month of
interview are ignored."* MICS does the same thing.

Two things follow that are easy to get wrong.

**The window is part of the published target, not a constant.** Reports choose
their own. Malawi 2000 and The Gambia 2019-20 publish 0--6 years before the
survey; the three Rwanda surveys publish 0--4. Running every survey on a single
window is the easiest way to fail a validation that would otherwise pass
exactly.

**The boundaries must be half-open, `[start, end)`.** This sounds like
hair-splitting and is not. Exposure in month `m` is counted when `start <= m`,
so if events are tested with `start < m` instead, a death in the very first
month of the window contributes exposure but cannot be counted as an event ---
the numerator and the denominator disagree about whether that month is in the
window. Of seven validation surveys spanning phases 2 to 8, **three were each
short by exactly one death**, and in every case it was a sibling who died in
month `doi - 84` exactly. With the half-open convention all seven reproduce the
reference exactly.

The same convention puts a death falling exactly on an age-group boundary into
the *later* group, which is what `floor((death - dob)/60)` does and what both
reference implementations assume.

*In this package:* `cell_config(time.periods = '7yr_beforeinterview')`, with
`time.offset = "doi"`. `make.time.periods()` builds other windows. The half-open
convention is in `window_intersect()`.


## 1.3 Exposure accounting

### Does the month of death count as exposure?

**The DHS says yes.** `AM_rates.do:711` sets `last = mm8` when a death falls
inside an interval, and exposure is then `last - first + 1` --- so the month of
death is included. A sibling is treated as having lived all the way through the
month she is reported to have died in.

This is one of the two places where the DHS and MICS references genuinely
disagree, and neither is wrong: it is a convention, not a fact. MICS stops the
month before (§2.3). With a half-open observation window, "through the month of
death" means an end-of-observation value of `death + 1`.

*In this package:* `death.exposure = "dhs"` (the default) on all three
`prep_*_sib_histories()` functions. Note for anyone constructing sibling data by
hand: this makes `sib.endobs` equal to `death + 1`, not `death`.

### Which age group does a death belong to?

Exposure is accumulated by walking each sibling's lifeline through five-year age
intervals, computed from her **date of birth** (`:693`, `first = mm4 + (i+2)*60`
for interval `i`). A death is assigned to the interval that contains it. It is
*not* assigned using the reported age at death (`mm7`), which can disagree with
the date arithmetic.

*In this package:* `cell_config(age.offset = "sib.dob")`.

### Birth and death dates

The DHS supplies both as century month codes: `mm4` date of birth, `mm8` date of
death. `AM_rates.do`'s header assumes they are *always* coded, and it has no
fallback.

In practice they are not quite always coded. The one exception found across all
43 surveys is a single sibling in Gabon 2012 whose `mm4` is missing but whose
current age is reported; recovering a date of birth from the reported age
retains 6.1 person-years of male exposure in 105,599, where the reference drops
him. Arguably recovering him is the better behaviour; either way, the
discrepancy is 0.006% and it is the *only* one across the whole sample.

If a survey does not supply the CMC dates, the derivations are the same ones
MICS needs, and §2.4 sets them out.

*In this package:* `get_sib_df()` uses `sib.dob` and `sib.death.date` where the
varmap supplies them, and derives them otherwise.


## 1.4 Cause and timing: what makes a death pregnancy-related

Everything in this section turns on a single coded item, `mm9`:

| `mm9` | Meaning | Pregnancy-related | Maternal |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | died while pregnant | yes | yes |
| 3 | died during delivery | yes | yes |
| 4 | since delivery --- never assigned in practice | yes | yes |
| 5 | within six weeks of a delivery | yes | yes |
| 6 | between six weeks and two months of a delivery | **yes** | **no** |

**Pregnancy-related** is `mm9` in 2--6 (`:725`), with **no cause exclusion of
any kind**. Code 6 is exactly what makes this the *two-month* quantity, and it
is precisely the line the reference draws between this and the maternal column.

**Maternal** is `mm9` in 2--5 and `mm16` not 1 or 2 (`:728`). Stopping at code 5
is exactly a 42-day cut, and `mm16` excludes deaths due to violence or an
accident.

Three details that look like edge cases and are not.

**`mm12` is not used at all.** `mm12` is the time-since-delivery band, and the
temptation is to use it to impose a timing window. The reference does not: its
header states plainly that *"mm12 is not needed"*, and it drops the column
before the roster is even reshaped (`:151`, `:298`). Applying an `mm12` band of
100--141 (0--41 days) on top of `mm9` --- which is a natural-looking mistake ---
imposes a 42-day cut on a quantity defined over two months, and applies a
*postpartum* timing test even to deaths that occurred during pregnancy or
delivery. On Rwanda 2010 that gives 51.2 pregnancy-related deaths against a
published 91.

**A missing `mm16` must count as "not an accident".** `mm16` is *not asked* when
the death occurred during delivery, so for `mm9 = 3` it is missing by design
rather than by non-response. In The Gambia 2019-20, all 40 in-window delivery
deaths have `mm16` missing and none of the `mm9 = 2` or `mm9 = 5` deaths do.
Requiring `mm16 == 0` would silently drop every delivery death.

**Code 4 is included even though it never occurs.** The reference tests a range,
not a set, and `mm9 = 4` is never assigned in any survey examined. Including it
costs nothing and matches the reference.

*In this package:* `add_maternal_deaths(style = "dhs")`, which calls
`is_preg_related_dhs()` and `is_maternal_dhs()`. Siblings who did not die of the
relevant cause get a death date of `-1` rather than `NA`, so that they still
contribute exposure; both columns are `NA` for male siblings.

### The `mm9` 5/6 split is a questionnaire artefact

This one constrains the *maternal* estimand rather than the pregnancy-related
one, and it is a property of the DHS definition rather than of any
implementation.

Codes 5 and 6 are not a reliable partition of postpartum deaths. Of the five
surveys that carry `mm16`, and so are the only ones where maternal mortality is
computable at all:

| Survey | `mm9` = 5 | `mm9` = 6 | |
|---|---|---|---|
| `GAIR71FL` Gabon | 14 | 1 | both bands used |
| `LBIR7AFL` Liberia | 23 | 7 | both bands used |
| `MLIR7AFL` Mali | 26 | 16 | both bands used |
| `GMIR81FL` Gambia 2019-20 | 68 | 8 | both bands used |
| **`ZAIR71FL` South Africa 2016** | **0** | **26** | **only code 6** |

South Africa 2016 recording zero deaths within six weeks of delivery and 26
between six weeks and two months is not credible as a description of a
population. It is much more likely that its questionnaire asked only about the
two-month window, so every postpartum death was coded 6. Where that happens,
`mm9 <= 5` drops *all* postpartum deaths, and the maternal count degenerates to
"died while pregnant or during delivery".

The consequence is that **maternal counts are not comparable across surveys that
code differently**. Pregnancy-related spans both codes and is insensitive to it,
which is a substantive argument for preferring pregnancy-related when comparing
across surveys --- quite apart from the fact that it is computable for all 43
and maternal for only five.

### The 2016 PRMR redefinition

`AM_rates.do:307-320` carries, **inside a comment block and therefore never
executed**, a rule introduced as *"Important for redefinition of Pregnancy
Related Mortality Ratio (PRMR) in surveys from 2016 onwards"*:

```
If mm9=2, and mm16=1 or 2, recode mm9 to 1
```

That is: a death *during pregnancy* reported as due to violence or an accident
stops counting as pregnancy-related. The DHS Program documents the rule (see
`blog.dhsprogram.com/mmr-prmr/`) but the code it ships does not apply it, so the
published figures produced with that code do not reflect it either.

So there are two defensible answers, and which one you want depends on whether
you are reproducing published tables or following the current definition. It can
only bite on the five surveys carrying `mm16`.

*In this package:*
`add_maternal_deaths(prmr.accident.recode = TRUE)` applies it; the default is
`FALSE`, which reproduces published tables.


## 1.5 Weights and age standardisation

### Weight scaling

`v005` is published **multiplied by 1,000,000**, so it must be divided by `1e6`
to recover weights that average 1.

This matters more than it looks, because it is a property of the DHS
specifically. Applying it to an already-normalised weight --- a MICS weight, or
a simulated one --- divides every weight by a million, and nothing downstream
complains.

*In this package:* `weight.scale`, which defaults to `1e6` for
`prep_dhs_sib_histories()` and `1` elsewhere.

### The all-woman factor

`AM_rates.do:551` weights the respondent age distribution by
`v005/1e6 * awfactt/100`, not by `v005/1e6` alone. `awfactt` is the all-woman
factor, which corrects the age distribution in surveys that interviewed only
ever-married women.

**In a survey of all women, `awfactt` is 100 and the factor is inert.** Checked
across all 44 DHS individual-recode files in the validation sample: 43 carry the
column, and in every one of them `awfactt` is exactly 100 for every respondent;
the remaining file (`CIIR51FL`, Côte d'Ivoire 2005) does not carry it at all. So
it makes no difference to any figure in this sample.

It would matter for an ever-married-women sample, and it is worth knowing that
the correction applies to the **age distribution used for standardisation**, not
to the exposure or death counts, which are weighted by `v005/1e6` alone.

*In this package:* not implemented. The DHS varmaps do not map `awfactt`, and
`get_ego_age_distn()` weights by the scaled `v005` only. For an all-women sample
this is exactly the reference behaviour.

### Which age distribution standardises the rates

This is the decision most likely to be got wrong from reading the reference
code, because **the reference code and the published reports appear to disagree**.

`get_age_distributions` at `AM_rates.do:450` takes the men's age distribution
from the men's recode (`MR`) file, or from the household (`PR`) file where there
was no men's survey. Read literally, that means a published male rate cannot be
reproduced from the women's file alone.

In practice it can. **Published DHS reports standardise both sexes by the age
distribution of the survey respondents** --- the interviewed women. Checked
against four published male rates spanning DHS phases 4 to 8:

| Survey | Respondents' distribution | `MR` distribution | Published |
|---|---|---|---|
| Malawi 2000 | 11.064 | 11.162 | **11.1** |
| Rwanda 2005 | **7.393** | 7.285 | **7.39** |
| Rwanda 2014-15 | **2.961** | 2.881 | **2.96** |
| Gambia 2019-20 | **3.133** | --- | **3.13** |

The respondents' distribution matches in all four, and the `MR`-derived one is
further away in every case where it can be computed.

So if you are reproducing a published table, use the respondents' age
distribution for both sexes. If you are reproducing the *current* `AM_rates.do`,
you need the `MR` or `PR` file.

*In this package:* `get_ego_age_distn(only_females = TRUE)`, which is what
`aggregate_maternal_estimates()` uses. `only_females = FALSE` returns a separate
distribution per respondent sex and warns when the sample has only one, since
applying one sex's age structure to another is exactly the silent error this
guards against.

### A note on unreliable targets

Two published tables in the surveys examined here should not be used to validate
anything.

**Rwanda 2010's summary rows.** Its age-specific cells reproduce exactly ---
deaths, exposure, pregnancy-related deaths, every age group, both sexes --- but
its totals fail in three independent ways: the "age-adjusted" rates match the
*crude* rates rather than the standardised ones despite the footnote; Table
16.4's total exposure prints 165,352 against age rows summing to 120,900, and
165,352 is exactly the seven-year figure, so that one cell came from a different
run than the rest of the table; and the report's own maternal mortality ratio of
476 is consistent with the standardised rate rather than with the rate printed
beside it.

**Gabon 2000 cannot be read with default encoding.** `haven::read_dta()` fails
outright with *"Unable to convert string to the requested encoding (invalid byte
sequence)"*; `encoding = "latin1"` reads it. Not a recoding decision, but it is
silent in the sense that a pipeline may drop the survey without anyone noticing.


## 1.6 The life table constant

Converting age-specific rates into $_{35}q_{15}$ needs $_na_x$, the average
years lived in an interval by those who die in it. The textbook value is 2.5.
**`AM_rates.do:1084-1085` uses 2.6**, and says so deliberately:

```
//See DHS Guide to Statistics for use of 2.4 rather than 2.5 in the following formula
gen q5=5*mx/(1+2.4*mx)
```

With $n = 5$, a denominator of $1 + 2.4\,m_x$ is $n_ax = 2.6$. The MICS syntax
uses the same value (§2.7), so both major sources agree against the textbook.

The difference is small --- about 0.2 per 1,000 on a $_{35}q_{15}$ of 200 ---
but published figures are rounded to integers, so it cannot be recovered by
comparing against them, and it is free to get right. On The Gambia 2019-20 Table
14.2, $n_ax = 2.6$ gives 113.51 and 124.37 against a published 114 and 124;
$n_ax = 2.5$ gives a women's figure that rounds to 113.

*In this package:* `nmx_to_nqx()` and `q15_to_50()`, both taking `nax` with a
default of 2.6.

# Part 2: MICS

MICS has run **two structurally different** mortality modules under the same
"MM" label, and only one of them is a sibling survival history.

| | MICS2 / MICS3 | MICS4 / MICS5 | MICS6 / MICS7 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Method | Indirect sisterhood | **Direct sibling history** | **Direct sibling history** |
| Usable here? | **No** | Yes | Yes |
| Questionnaire | Household | Individual Women | Individual Women |
| Brothers enumerated? | No --- sisters only | Yes | Yes |
| Roster numbering | --- | `MM4`--`MM14` | `MM14`--`MM28` |
| Data file | inside `hl.sav` | dedicated `mm.sav` | dedicated `mm.sav` |
| Reference period | ~10--14 years | 7 years | 7 years |

MICS2 and MICS3 collect summary sisterhood counts in the household
questionnaire, sisters only, with no per-sibling roster and no ages at death.
There is nothing for a direct estimator to consume.

Three practical points before any recoding.

**The module is optional and rarely fielded.** It appears in MICS7's
*Complementary Questionnaire Topics*, not the Base Questionnaire. Of **229**
MICS surveys scanned, only **13** have a usable sibling roster: 2 in MICS4, 7 in
MICS5, 4 in MICS6, none in MICS7.

**Presence of `mm.sav` is the definitive test**, and a survey lacking it does
not hide the roster in `wm.sav` --- checked directly on six such surveys, all of
which have zero `MM`-prefixed variables in the women's file. Beware one trap:
**MICS3's `mm.sav` is the *men's* file**, not maternal mortality. It contains
`MM4` "Man's Line number" and `mmweight` "men's sample weight". Any inventory
built by globbing for `mm.sav` picks up three false positives.

**The roster is long, not wide.** Unlike the DHS, MICS publishes `mm.sav` with
one row per reported sibling, so there is no reshape to do. Zimbabwe 2019 is
47,835 rows by 48 variables.

Country customisation is real and has to be tolerated rather than assumed away:
variable counts across the usable surveys range from 23 to 48, Pakistan Sindh
adds an item and drops the imputed CMC dates, and only 4 of the 13 carry a `psu`
column.


## 2.1 Which reported siblings enter the analysis

### Sex

`MM15` (`MM5` in MICS4/5) is coded 1 male, 2 female, with 8 and 9 for don't know
and no response. The same hazard as the DHS applies, and for the same reason:
any shortcut that maps "not 2" to male silently turns unusable codes into men.

### Survival status --- and a real divergence

`MM16` (`MM6` in MICS4/5) is coded **1 yes, 2 no, 8 don't know**. Note that this
is *not* the DHS coding: DHS `mm2` is 1 alive, **0** dead. Passing MICS codes
through a pipeline that expects the DHS convention drops every dead sibling as
though its survival status were missing, which drives every mortality estimate
to zero.

⚠ **UNICEF keeps siblings whose survival status is unknown, with full
exposure.** The DHS reference drops them. This is a genuine difference between
the two, and it is small but not zero.

Iraq 2018 has **81 male** such siblings against **21 female** --- respondents
evidently know less about brothers --- and the published exposure sits *between*
the two treatments:

| | Female exposure | Male exposure |
|---|---|---|
| Dropping them | 471,232 (−62) | 485,061 (−337) |
| Keeping them with full exposure | 471,342 (+48) | 485,495 (+97) |
| **Published** | **471,294** | **485,398** |

So MICS neither drops them nor carries them to the interview date: it censors
them somewhere in between, or drops the subset whose age is also unknown.
Reproducing that exactly would mean guessing the censoring rule. The whole
spread is under 0.1% of exposure and does not move any rate to two decimal
places. Deaths are unaffected either way, since a sibling with unknown survival
status contributes no death.

*In this package:* `recode_mics_sib_vars()` maps `MM16` 1 to alive, 2 to dead,
8/9 to `NA`. Unknown-survival siblings are dropped unless
`keep_missing = TRUE`, which is the DHS convention rather than the MICS one.

### Don't-know codes on numeric items

⚠ **This is the single most dangerous MICS-specific recode.** MICS codes
don't-know and no-response on the *numeric* sibling items as **98 and 99**, not
as system-missing:

| Item | DK/NR values | Cross-check against published DQ.7.1 |
|---|---|---|
| `MM17` age of living sibling | 99 × 180 | "Age of living siblings: Missing/DK **180**" |
| `MM18` years since death | 98 × 95, 99 × 57 | |
| `MM19` age at death | 98 × 96, 99 × 67 | both DK = **102**, published **102** |

(Zimbabwe 2019.) Passed through as real values these are silently catastrophic:
a sibling with an age at death of 98 gets a date of birth 98 years before her
death, and a living sibling aged 99 falls outside every age group.

The damage is **masked whenever MICS supplies its own imputed CMC dates**,
because then the derivations that would consume these values never fire. That is
why the problem is easy to miss: it does nothing at all in the surveys where the
CMC columns are complete, and is severe in the one survey (Bhutan 2010) that
ships no CMC columns.

*In this package:* `recode_mics_sib_vars()` sets 98 and 99 to `NA` across
`sib.age`, `sib.death.yrsago`, `sib.death.age`,
`sib.days.postpartum.death` and `sib.num.children`, and reports how many.


## 2.2 The observation window

The MICS syntax uses `kmin = 84`, `kmax = 1` relative to `wdoi`, i.e. the window
`[wdoi - 84, wdoi - 1]` --- the 84 months ending the month before the interview.
This is identical to the DHS window, and the month of interview is excluded in
both.

No MICS document states whether the seven years are years-since-death 0--6 or
1--7, so this was settled empirically against the published exposure column:

| Candidate window | Ratio to published exposure |
|---|---|
| `[doi - 84, doi)` --- **0--6 completed years** | **0.9966** |
| `[doi - 96, doi - 12)` --- 1--7 years | 0.9861 |
| shifted one month | 0.9958 |

0--6 wins. MICS chose a seven-year window specifically "to reduce possible
heaping of reported years since death on five-year intervals", which is worth
knowing when comparing derived dates against DHS CMC values.

The half-open boundary convention of §1.2 applies identically here.


## 2.3 Exposure accounting

### Does the month of death count as exposure?

⚠ **MICS says no.** The syntax sets `higcm = MM18C - 1`: exposure stops the
month *before* death. The DHS counts the month of death (§1.3).

This is a real difference between the two references, not an error in either,
and it is the second of the two ⚠ rows in the decision index that a combined
DHS/MICS analysis has to resolve deliberately.

Its size is small and measurable. On Madagascar 2018 --- the one validation
survey with almost no unknown-survival siblings to confound the comparison ---
the MICS convention reproduces the published female exposure of **202,959
exactly**, against 203,010 under the DHS convention.

*In this package:* `death.exposure = c("dhs", "mics")` on all three
`prep_*_sib_histories()` functions. The default is `"dhs"`, which is what the
package has always done --- so reproducing a published MICS exposure figure
means asking for `"mics"` explicitly.

### Which age group does a death belong to?

As with the DHS: the age group holding at the month of death, computed from the
date of birth, not the reported age at death.


## 2.4 Birth and death dates

MICS6 usually ships `MM17C` and `MM18C`, imputed CMC dates of birth and death;
MICS4/5 ships `MM7C` and `MM8C`. **Some countries ship neither** --- Bhutan 2010
is the only survey in the archive with no CMC columns at all, and Pakistan Sindh
2018-19 drops them too. So an implementation must be able to derive them.

The derivations assume a death or birth halfway through the reported year:

| Target | Derivation | MICS6 input |
|---|---|---|
| Date of death | `doi - (12 * yrsago + 6)` | `MM18` years ago |
| Date of birth, living sibling | `doi - (12 * age + 6)` | `MM17` current age |
| Date of birth, dead sibling | `death.date - 12 * death.age` | `MM19` age at death |

Note the third one is guarded on **age at death**, which is what the arithmetic
actually uses. Guarding it on years-since-death instead --- an easy slip, since
that is what the second derivation needs --- silently produces a missing date of
birth for any sibling with a known age at death but no years-since-death.

Where both are available, the derived and supplied dates can be compared
directly. Dropping the CMC columns from Zimbabwe 2019 deliberately and deriving
instead gives a date of birth correlating **0.9999** with MICS's own `MM17C`,
which both validates the derivation and shows how wrong it was before the 98/99
codes were handled.

One sanity check worth building in: a derived date of birth implying an age at
interview no human reaches means the reported years-since-death and age at death
are jointly inconsistent. Bhutan 2010 has a sibling reported as dying 58 years
ago at age 58, implying a birth 116 years before the interview. Note this is
*not* the same as a sibling dying before the respondent was born, which is
perfectly possible and not rare where sibships are long.

*In this package:* `get_sib_df()` uses supplied dates when the varmap maps them
and derives otherwise; `max.plausible.age` (default 110) controls the warning.


## 2.5 Cause and timing: what makes a death pregnancy-related

Where the DHS uses one coded item, MICS asks **three separate binaries**, plus a
day count, plus two cause items:

| MICS6 | MICS4/5 | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `MM22` | `MM10` | pregnant when she died |
| `MM23` | `MM11` | died during childbirth |
| `MM24` | `MM12` | died within two months of the end of a pregnancy |
| `MM25` | --- | days after the end of the pregnancy |
| `MM26` | --- | died of violence |
| `MM27` | --- | died of an accident |

MICS4/5 has no day count and no cause items, so it supports **pregnancy-related
mortality only**, like DHS phases 2--6. MICS6/7 supports both estimands, like
DHS phase 7 and later.

**Pregnancy-related, two-month window:** `MM22 = 1` or `MM23 = 1` or
`MM24 = 1`, with no cause exclusion.

**Pregnancy-related, 42-day window:** as above but with `MM24 = 1 & MM25 < 42`.

**Maternal:** the 42-day window, additionally excluding `MM26 = 1` or
`MM27 = 1`. MICS6/7 only.

### ⚠ Published MICS tables do not report maternal deaths

This is the most consequential single finding in this document for anyone
comparing against published MICS figures.

MICS reports print a table headed *Maternal mortality*, with a column labelled
"Maternal Deaths", and a footnote defining a maternal death as one occurring
*"from any cause except accidents or violence"*. **UNICEF's own tabulation
syntax computes something else.** It flags a death with

```
if (MM15 = 2 & (MM22 = 1 or MM23 = 1 or (MM24 = 1 and MM25 < 42))) md = 1.
```

and never reads `MM26` or `MM27` anywhere in the file. So the published column
is a **pregnancy-related** count on a **42-day** window --- which is the WHO
definition of a pregnancy-related death, and not what the footnote says.

Iraq 2018 settles it, because it reproduces to within 1% on every other quantity
in the same table:

| | Ours | Published | Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|
| Female exposure | 471,232 | 471,294 | 1.0000 |
| Male exposure | 485,061 | 485,398 | 0.9993 |
| Female all-cause deaths | 574 | 574 | 1.0007 |
| Male all-cause deaths | 1,158 | 1,158 | 0.9996 |
| **TM.9.3, as pregnancy-related, 42-day** | **64.9** | **64.4** | **1.008** |
| TM.9.3, as maternal | 54.2 | 64.4 | 0.848 |

TM.9.3 prints death counts as integers, so the published figure appears in the
report as 64; the 64.4 used here is the unrounded value recovered from the
published proportion of female deaths. Either way the contrast is the same size:
the pregnancy-related reading lands within 1%, the maternal reading 15% low.

So the report's *methodology text* --- which says pregnancy-related --- is
authoritative, and the table footnote is stale boilerplate. The narrative text
in MICS6 reports still says "pregnancy-related deaths" in places, which is the
correct description, not the leftover.

*In this package:* compare against `sib.preg_related.death.date` with
`add_maternal_deaths(style = "mics6", preg.window = "42days")`, **not**
`sib.maternal.death.date`. The default is `preg.window = "2months"`, so
reproducing a published MICS figure means asking for `"42days"` explicitly.

### Three skip patterns that must be in the recode

All three come from the questionnaire routing, and all three silently change
counts if missed.

**1. `MM23 = 1` skips `MM26` and `MM27` entirely.** A childbirth death is
unconditionally maternal, and the cause items are `NA` *by design* for it. A
test written with `==` propagates that `NA` and drops the death; a membership
test (`%in%`, or an explicit `is.na()` guard) does not.

**2. `MM21` routes sisters who died before age 12 past `MM22`--`MM25`.** Those
items are `NA` by design too. Without an explicit age guard --- and with a
policy of treating missing timing as inside the window --- every under-12 female
death becomes maternal.

But the guard has to be written as **"not *known* to have died under 12"**, not
"known to have died at 12 or over". A sister whose age at death was reported as
don't-know (`MM19 = 98`) becomes missing once the 98/99 codes are handled, and
the stricter test then drops her even when she answered `MM22`--`MM24`
affirmatively --- which is itself proof she was asked. That cost 7
pregnancy-related deaths in Iraq 2018 and 5 in Zimbabwe 2019.

**3. `MM16 = don't know` jumps to the next sibling** --- no age, no dates,
nothing. Those rows carry no information at all.

### The missing-day-count decision

`MM25` is asked only of sisters who died within two months (`MM24 = 1`). When it
is missing, something has to decide whether she falls inside the 42-day maternal
window. There is no right answer; it is a choice about the estimand.

Its size, across three MICS6 surveys: **5 of 38 such deaths in Iraq 2018, and
none at all in Zimbabwe 2019 or Madagascar 2018**. It moves only the maternal
column, never the pregnancy-related one --- so it does not affect any comparison
against a published table, which reports pregnancy-related.

Worth noting alongside it: MICS has **no don't-know code on `MM17`, `MM18`,
`MM19` or `MM25`**, so missing there really is missing rather than an explicit
refusal.

*In this package:* `na.action`, which has **no default** for the MICS styles ---
`add_maternal_deaths()` errors and explains the choice rather than picking one.

### ⚠ `MM16` means opposite things in MICS and the DHS

In MICS6, `MM16` is **"Is (name) still alive?"**. In DHS phase 7 and later,
`mm16` is **"died of violence or an accident"**. Mapping one onto the other
turns survival status into cause of death.

MICS6 loop control is `MM28`, not `MM16`. `MM20` and `MM21` are interviewer
check items and do not appear in the data at all.

Two smaller numbering traps in the same area: the MICS6 roster is `MM15`--`MM19`
and the pregnancy items are `MM22`--`MM24`, whereas MICS4/5 uses `MM5`--`MM9`
and `MM10`--`MM12`. And `sib.num.children` (MICS4/5 `MM13`) was **dropped in
MICS6** entirely.

*In this package:* `check_mics_varmap()` refuses to run any MICS varmap that
maps `mm16` to an accident or violence item.


## 2.6 Weights and age standardisation

**Weights are already normalised.** `wmweight` averages 1. Do not apply DHS-style
scaling.

**Age standardisation uses the interviewed women**, which the MICS methodology
text states and which the syntax confirms. This was worth checking because two
other authorities describe something else --- IUSSP says women aged 15--49 in
the surveyed households, MMEIG says the female population of respondent
households. Standardising Zimbabwe 2019's all-cause female rate by the
respondents gives **6.27 against a published 6.28**.

One detail: the syntax restricts the age distribution to women with a
**completed interview** (`WM17 = 1`). Since the sibling roster comes from
completed interviews anyway, this rarely differs, but it is the exact rule.

*In this package:* `weight.scale = 1` is the default for
`prep_mics_sib_histories()`. `get_ego_age_distn()` builds the distribution from
the respondents present in the prepped data; it does not filter on `WM17`.


## 2.7 The life table constant

The MICS syntax computes

```
compute fqx = 1 - ( 5 * (adfmr/1000) / (1+2.4*(adfmr/1000)) ).
```

which is $n_ax = 2.6$, the same as the DHS --- **even though the syntax file's
own header documents 2.5**. Where the header and the code disagree, the code is
what produced the published tables.


## 2.8 Two published MICS targets that are unreliable

**Zimbabwe 2019's female figures.** It fails to reproduce on *every* quantity,
including ones involving no maternal recode at all: exposure 0.997, female
all-cause deaths 0.987, pregnancy-related deaths 0.896. Its **male** columns
reproduce exactly through the same code, which is why the pattern cannot come
from the calculation. The report also contradicts itself --- its sampling-error
appendix gives a maternal mortality ratio of 413.64 against 462 in TM.9.3, and
it is the appendix that reproduces (409.9). Zimbabwe *2014* reproduces closely,
so this is not a country-level problem.

**A units footnote that disagrees with itself.** A MICS6 footnote says "per
100,000 women 15--49" while the table footnote says "per 1,000 woman-years". The
printed column is per 1,000.

**And one comparison not to make:** Zimbabwe 2014's published figure of 614 and
2019's of 462 are on different estimands, different windows and different cause
exclusions. They are not a trend.

---

# Part 3: Where the two instruments disagree

Most of the decisions above have the same answer on both sides. Three do not,
and all three matter if DHS and MICS surveys go into one analysis.

### 1. The published pregnancy-related series are on different windows

This is the important one, and it is easy to miss because both are called
"pregnancy-related".

* **A published DHS pregnancy-related count is a two-month quantity** --- `mm9`
  in 2--6, which explicitly includes deaths between six weeks and two months
  after delivery.
* **A published MICS pregnancy-related count is a 42-day quantity** ---
  `MM24 = 1 & MM25 < 42`, which explicitly excludes them.

So reproducing both published series means using *different* definitions, and
putting the two on one footing means departing from at least one published
table. Neither choice is wrong, but it has to be made deliberately and reported:

| Goal | DHS | MICS |
|---|---|---|
| Reproduce published tables | as published (two-month) | `preg.window = "42days"` |
| One consistent two-month series | as published | `preg.window = "2months"` |
| One consistent 42-day series | not directly available from `mm9` | `preg.window = "42days"` |

Note the gap in the bottom row: a 42-day *pregnancy-related* count is not
directly identifiable from `mm9` in every DHS survey, because whether a survey
codes postpartum deaths as 5 or 6 is a questionnaire property (§1.4). Where a
survey used only code 6, the 42-day cut removes all postpartum deaths rather
than the ones beyond 42 days.

### 2. The month of death

The DHS counts it as exposure; MICS stops the month before. Sub-0.1% on any one
survey, but systematic and in one direction. Pick one convention for a combined
analysis rather than inheriting whichever the source happened to use.

### 3. Siblings with unknown survival status

The DHS drops them; MICS keeps them with full exposure, and the published
figures suggest UNICEF actually does something in between. The effect is under
0.1% of exposure and is larger for men than for women, because respondents know
less about brothers.

### What both agree on

Worth stating, since it is easy to assume more divergence than there is: the
seven-year window and the exclusion of the interview month; assigning a death to
the age group holding at the month of death rather than by reported age at
death; standardising by the age distribution of the interviewed respondents; and
$n_ax = 2.6$ in the life table.

### What will not reproduce from either source, by design

* **Confidence intervals.** DHS fits Poisson models and reports log-scale
  intervals; MICS uses jackknife replication with ±2 standard errors; this
  package bootstraps and reports percentile intervals. All three are defensible
  and none agree. Note also that the DHS sampling-error appendix for maternal
  mortality comes from a *separate* CSPro application rather than from
  `AM_rates.do`, and in Zimbabwe 2019 the two disagree with each other by 11%.
* **The maternal mortality ratio.** MMR is the age-standardised rate divided by
  a general fertility rate from the women's birth history --- a different module
  entirely. Both replicas in `data-raw/` compute it, for validation only.
* **Subpopulation rates.** The DHS Program explicitly declines to compute
  maternal mortality within subpopulations, so there is nothing to compare
  against.
* **The individual-visibility estimator.** `asdr.ind` appears in no published
  table by construction; it is what this package exists to add. The estimator
  that should reproduce published figures is `asdr.agg`, which is
  $\sum w \cdot \text{deaths} / \sum w \cdot \text{exposure}$ with no visibility
  weighting --- exactly the conventional DHS and MICS calculation. If `asdr.agg`
  does not reproduce, something in the pipeline is wrong; if `asdr.ind` differs,
  that is the finding.
